Spacebase DF-9 is a colony management simulation developed by Double Fine Productions and published by Double Fine Productions, later distributed on Steam under Xbox Game Studios. Set in a distant future where humanity has spread across the stars, the game casts players as the administrator of an isolated space station tasked with housing settlers, managing resources, and surviving the countless dangers of life in deep space. Its concept is immediately appealing: build a thriving orbital community from a handful of rooms and personnel, then watch as its inhabitants create stories of friendship, tragedy, and survival. Even years after its release, the title remains an intriguing example of a game built on an exceptional premise.

The gameplay centers on constructing and maintaining a space station piece by piece. Players begin with a modest outpost and gradually expand it into a bustling habitat complete with sleeping quarters, recreational areas, infirmaries, security offices, and industrial facilities. Oxygen management, power distribution, and resource collection are constant concerns, ensuring that every expansion carries risks alongside rewards. Nearby asteroids can be mined for valuable materials, while abandoned ships drifting through space provide opportunities for scavenging. These mechanics create a satisfying loop of exploration, construction, and maintenance that encourages players to think several steps ahead.

One of Spacebase DF-9's greatest strengths is its ability to generate memorable scenarios through its simulation systems. Colonists develop personalities and react to the environment around them, creating moments that feel surprisingly personal. A station may operate smoothly for hours before an unexpected meteor strike breaches a critical corridor, causing a chain reaction of panic and decompression. Hostile intruders, alien infestations, and equipment failures add further unpredictability, transforming ordinary management tasks into desperate attempts to save the colony. The game's dark humor shines throughout these moments, giving even catastrophic failures an oddly entertaining quality.

Visually, the game adopts a clean and colorful presentation that makes managing a growing station relatively easy. Individual characters are simple in design but expressive enough to convey their actions and emotions. Watching crews move between departments and interact with one another adds life to the station, while the ambient soundtrack reinforces the feeling of being stranded in an endless expanse of space. The user interface is straightforward, allowing players to focus on building and responding to emergencies without becoming overwhelmed by excessive complexity.

Unfortunately, Spacebase DF-9 is equally known for its unrealized potential. Originally released through Early Access, the game generated considerable excitement due to its ambitious roadmap and the reputation of its developer. However, many of the promised systems never reached completion, leaving the final release feeling smaller in scope than players expected. Certain mechanics lack depth, and progression eventually reveals limitations in artificial intelligence and station management. Rather than evolving into a definitive colony simulator, the game often feels like a snapshot of a much larger vision that never fully came together.

That lingering sense of incompleteness ultimately defines the experience. There is still enjoyment to be found in building a functioning settlement among the stars and witnessing the emergent stories that arise from its systems. Players who appreciate sandbox management games may discover several entertaining hours within its framework, particularly if they approach it with tempered expectations. Yet it is difficult to ignore how much more Spacebase DF-9 could have been had its development continued. It stands as both an entertaining simulation and a reminder that compelling ideas alone are not always enough to fulfill ambitious promises.

If you’re here on a historical tour of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of mismanagement, I would highly recommend the game “Space Haven”, which is feature-complete, well-executed, and supported by developers who care more about their customers than their own ego. It’s what this game could’ve been.

I think my experience with this game was like many. Encouraged by some excellent Early Access titles at the time, when Spacebase DF-9 hit early access, I naively assumed that I was buying something that would be worked on for years. Double Fine had published an exciting development plan. However, just a few months later, development was abruptly stopped, and the still very minimal, bug-riddled game was released as 1.0, with future plans quietly and unceremoniously removed.

In the fallout, Double Fine made statements claiming that they broke no promises and they simply weren’t making enough money on the game - which, honestly, never reached a state where it was functional enough to be worth buying.

My Steam Early Access purchase, like everybody who bought the game, was seen by Double Fine as a donation.

Note, at the time of abandonment, if I remember correctly, Steam Refunds were not a thing. If players were able to claim steam refunds, I doubt they would’ve even said anything.

It’s really a shame, as this was a game that had a ton of potential, and instead, it was simply the game that made me forever mistrustful of early access. Even a decade down the line, after formally abandoning the game and releasing code to the community, who fixed the game for free, Double Fine still has the audacity to claim DF-9 as a complete project that they have no shame charging for.

Double Fine has recently become an independent studio again. I have serious doubts that they will survive, given Tim Schafer’s now mile-long streak of financial negligence. He and the studio paint their players not as customers, but as charitable supporters patronizing their passion projects until they get bored and move onto a new one. They truly just don’t care as long as they get to make “their next game”.

Spacebase DF-9 is an extremely promising looking sci-fi base building/strategy game... and there's a huge market for such games if done right, which this isn't.  In fact this is a cautionary tale about not judging a book by it's cover... and while the traditional meaning of that is we shouldn't dismiss a book just because it looks bad, when it comes to video games, it's the opposite.  Some video games may look really fantastic but turn out to be duds... especially when they're not even complete games.

How did it come to this?

The core problem here is that this isn't a sincerely made, professional game, it's a Game Jam/demo project.  Game Jam and other student/project games are not made for gamers, they're made for the benefit of stroking the ego of developers.  It's obviously not possible for a game slapped together over a few days to be of the same quality as a properly, sincerely made game from a full development team with a full budget who take the right amount of time and put in genuine hard work to create a product for gamers.  Sure, it is possible to slap together a game in such a manner, unprofessionally.  This is a lot like driving a car using only your feet.  Just because it can be done, doesn't mean it's a good idea, and often ends up in disaster.

After the game jam, Double Fine made a commitment to finish the game... then didn't bother, they just abandoned it.  They took all the money from gamers based on this promise, abandoned the game, and kept all the cash they scammed out of gamers.  Completely reprehensible. 

Reviewing SteamDB to check how popular this game was with players reveals a surprise... there's a very healthy spike in player counts for the game.  How is this possible, if the game is incomplete and unplayable?  This only happened once, around the same time that trading cards were applied to the game... so this is just card idlers getting their cards and moving on.  A closer look at the numbers shows the game just has a couple of players every week running up the game and idling it for cards, then deleting it.  We must ask how it benefits gamers for there to be so many games like this, with no merit as a serious game, that only generate sales from people idling and selling the trading cards.

The developer is deliberately and unethically trying to scam gamers into paying them the greedy, cash grab price of $10 USD for a game they know is broken.  Don't give it to them.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

Well the studio he was in charge of by the name of "Doublefine" had a period I like to call the "Indie phase" where they hosted game jams and picked the best games out of the ones on display to be made into fully fledged games. One of the games they picked came out somewhat half baked. It was called "Broken age" and was forced to launch with only half of the game playable, so the studio could make enough money off the sales to create the second half of the game and add that. 
This might not seem so bad until you realise that the company had made a kickstarter for that game and promised the backers a full and ready game if they backed it. So understandably many backers were upset about this.

But Broken age wasn't the game that got the rawest deal. That was this game Spacebase DF-9. While I didn't back it on its kickstarter (Yes there was a kickstarter for this game too) I did buy it in early access. Now thankfully the game is playable.
Its a quirky yet fun space colony management sim where you get to make choices that effect your colony now and then.

But there is a glaring flaw here and it is the reason I cannot recommend the game. Because the whole project was dropped like a hot potato, there is a point in the game where the progression and content grinds to a halt. And I don't mean you get drip fed more content, I'm talking about walking into a fully fledged brick wall.

Your colonies/bases will be doomed eventually because of this. They may thrive, they might become sprawling megacentres that act as a refuge for humanity. But eventually they will wither and die due to enough natural space born disasters popping up and screwing the place over. I also encountered a game breaking scripting error once.
I was constantly choosing a dialogue option that sent attacking forces of pirate raiders away, and all of a sudden, something gave way in the code. 

Every single pirate raider I had convinced to leave my colony alone came swarming in like a bunch of army ants. That save file stood no chance. Everyone died horribly. 
In the end I'm sorry if my review made you upset, because to be honest I was getting upset while writing this. This game could have been great, but its been left behind.


Please, don't buy this game. Its not worth it in the end. 
Also for my final note I wouldn't recommend buying anything else from double fine either considering their track record. Except psychonaughts 2. I heard that is a really good game.

Anyway, that is everything I had to say.

In summary, Spacebase DF-9 certainly has potential and will appeal to fans of simulation games. But the lack of depth and the presence of bugs can frustrate the gameplay.

Sorry to say but this game just isn't finished and never will be. The beginning half of the game feels great but as you play you encounter more and more issues that make it impossible to play. Combat is the most broken, impossible system I have ever seen in any simulation game, ever. Let's talk about some issues:

-Derelicts (ships that spawn with loot / enemies) if you explore them, you're almost guaranteed to have a crewmate get stuck there and slowly suffocate and starve. Since you can't directly control anyone, the only way to save them to to build a path from the derelict to your ship. Also, it is functionally impossible to order your crew to fully explore a Derelict. They just won't do it.
-Incapacited crew/raiders can stay that way for so long that they'll literally starve to death. Additionally, enemies can just stand up and be completely fine afterward and go on a rampage, so if a raider goes down but doesn't die, you have to deploy security for them for weeks at a time.
-You can get pop-ups for events / problems that have been solved. These pop-ups never go away and will eventually open back up no matter what.
-I've lost several new games simply because my crew won't go inside and refill their oxygen. This has a risk of happening with every new game.
-Raiders can be ridiculously strong, able to kill (with only one raider) over 15 crew without being downed. Even if your entire crew is security you'll probably die to what is effectively a bad rng roll.
-Corpses never go away. The community patch fixes this but parasite corpses aren't removed.
-If one of your crew dies on a derelict, your crew will all automatically go to try to loot their body. If the derelict isn't empty of enemies, this means that your entire crew will eventually die trying to get loot. There is no way to stop them from doing this. 
-There's not prioritization of tasks. Even if your crew is literally dying and need to act immediately, they'll still stop to chat and ask people their favorite bands.
-Wounded crewmates will continue doing harmful tasks even to certain death. You can order them to go to the infirmary, but they don't listen and will die anyway.
-In the community patch, meteors will hit parts of your station. You get a warning and opportunity to avoid it, but you can't order your crew to move away so it's really just a random 'these crew members die' event. The game is FULL of these.
-Music just sometimes stops playing completely until you go into the menu and turn it up.
-Practically speaking, it's near impossible to catch illnesses and there's literally nothing you can do to change the result besides employing more doctors, so this event also serves as a 'these crew members die' random pop-up. The base game also has way too many random diseases to look out for, and each of them needs to be researched to effectively stop them, and research takes nearly 10 hours of real time per disease. This is faster with more researchers but everyone in this game just dies randomly with no ability to stop it.


Basically, this game is an embarrassment and is not really a game in its current state. It is an RNG button with some slight amount of interactivity but gives you so little control and has so little content that appears so often that functionally, the only thing you actually control in this game is heavily repeated dialogue that determines how many crew members you hire once every 2-5 minutes. Since your entire crew is likely to die about every 5 minutes, really these dialogues don't represent a choice at all, since you have to hire more to keep playing the game. In other words, this is a management sim where in reality, you are a passive participant that is watching events as they transpire.

This isn't a finished product, it's barely a game. It shouldn't be on sale at this point.

I decided to start going through some old games in my inventory and see how they are.  This was a game that I really enjoyed while it was in development. A non-ascii Space Dwarf Fortress?  Sounded good, and adding that DF suggested if not outright promised a deep and compelling world unfolding as you played.  

I looked at the store, it was $10 and mostly negative due to being released unfinished and abandoned.  Double Fine allowed feature creep and ambitions to overwhelm them and decided instead of pretending they would work on a project that had grown larger then they felt they would ever be able to do, they would instead release it as is and stop support for the game.  This plan was (I suspect) so they as a newer studio would be able to move on to other games and not be bogged down on an endless development cycle with a single game.  

How is this game?  It is (imo) 100% an unfinished Spacebase Startopoia.  It has a very similar feel and honestly doesn't look that old.  As it stands you will get overwhelmed with people just moving into your base and chewing up resources until everyone dies.  You'll get endless waves of pirates and derelicts until everyone dies, and you'll have builders brick themselves off into rooms and suffocate if you don't watch their every step.  

The game is compelling before everything goes to awry.  And that chaos that unfolds can be fun trying to get on top of it to start with, but it is never ending and dooms most playthroughs to failure.  It isn't that it is too hard, it is just unfinished with ideas implemented before they were worked into actual mechanics.  

I doubt it will as most everyone pretends this game never existed, but should it ever find its way to a sale of 50% or more it is worth $5 to see how long you can hold of the forces of chaos!

Spacebase DF-9… oh boy, what a backstory this game has… It started as a humble pitch in Amnesia Fortnight 2012, and the idea got enough votes to be made into a playable prototype in just 14 days. Not only that, it even got greenlighted to be made into a full game. So far so good. The game went into Steam Early Access, which is something I am always skeptical about, but as long as the game eventually gets fully released, I don’t really mind. But suddenly, the developers pulled the plug, and magically the game was finished and out of Early Access. What sorcery was this? Obviously, the game was still unfinished, with some crap responses from the publisher. To make matters worse, they released the source code, a middle finger saying that the community can and should finish the job.
Now, to be fair, it’s a sad story, but in the end what matters is the game itself right? Well, it’s a space management title, a genre I’m not really a fan of. But alright. The game starts with you picking a location to build a base, which basically acts as a difficulty select screen. Ok. It even has a special one designed to be a tutorial. Ok. Let’s try the tutorial then. I managed to complete it, and immediately saw how clunky it is to play. Navigation between menus is a mess and time consuming. After the tutorial things get worse. Plenty of times the crew members just ignore your orders or take forever to do anything. At this point I almost gave up on the game, but there is an unofficial community patch that essentially fixes a lot of bugs and adds some more features.
That patch is the supposed community salvation for the game, but even that one seems abandoned. Still, props for the people that spent time trying to fix and finish this mess of a game. Truth be said that patch really improves the overall experience, and I managed to play some playthroughs for a few hours this time. Unfortunately, the crappy foundation is still there, and it’s just a meh game. In the end, I just cannot recommend this: official release is unfinished, crappy publisher decision and PR, and even the community can’t save this disaster. While it is playable with the unofficial patch, I still didn’t like Spacebase DF-9. It’s just an average space management title, and there are way better titles in the genre that deserve more of your time and money.

I also had no idea that his development plan was *entirely contingent* on the absurdly optimistic presumption that this game would equal the financial backing of Prison Architect, one of the most successful projects ever to be released through Steam's Early Access program (by a studio which, it must also be said, allocated funds cautiously and responsibly, rather than haemorrhaging cash with nothing to show for it).

The fact that they splurged all their funding without coming close to completing the game would be bad enough, but the insult of slapping a 1.0 on an unfinished project (and the ludicrous claim by Schafer that he actually considers the game complete) is a kick in the teeth. Make no mistake - this is a deeply unsatisfying, barely playable mess, and to sell it under the pretence of having finished development is as shameless as it is reprehensible. More galling, there was clear potential for an excellent game here, so abandoning development wasn't merely an act of utter disregard for those of us who supported it, but also a foolish lost opportunity.

Not only should you *not even consider* buying this, but you shouldn't buy *anything* from a studio that treats its customers with such contempt.

Magnetic Fields determine the presence of derelect ships to investigate.

Base management games already aren't for everyone.  Even for those who like the genre, Spacebase DF-9 can be difficult to enjoy.

Right from the get-go, Spacebase-DF9 doesn't do much to "wow" you.  There are no cinematics or anything, and aside from possibly wanting to change Options, you'll quickly find yourself at a map of the galaxy, to choose where to start your base.  Depending on which coordinates you choose, relevant factors to your gameplay can differ - Stellar Density, which affects both how many resources there are and how frequently asteroids will hit your base - Warpgate Proximity, which affects how frequently you'll get visitors, wanted and otherwise - Threat Factor, which determines the frequency of Raider attacks - and Magnetic Interference, which determines the frequency of derelict vessels appearing.

Even at the first screen of "actual" gameplay, I have three issues with the game.  One, that your typical "difficulty" settings are pretty much thrown out the window.  You'd think that "low threat" would just be easy mode, but the threats still increase exponentially - I'll go into greater detail below.  Two, that there are a few different variables with which to basically "seed" your corner of the galaxy, but rather than let the player outright pick them, if you have particular settings you want, you have to scour the galaxy, pixel by pixel (okay, each area is maybe like 3 pixels wide, but it's still a huge area), until you find a spot you like.  If you want to force the player to try something new with each new game (which I'd be okay with, especially since this isn't exactly a "difficulty" setting), then just make it random, but it shouldn't be such a tedious process.  Third, why not tie Threat to Magnetic Frequency?  Raiders and derelict ships should go hand-in-hand, whether the ships are derelict due to Raider attacks, or the Raiders are there to loot the ships.  This would better fit the double-edge-sword nature of the other variables.

Something I mentioned above, and only becomes more prevalent the more you start to actually play the game, is that there is no story.  There are no cinematics, no voice acting, no plot, no progression from one stage to another.  You just survive in your base until you can no longer survive.  Many story-light games will still give you hints of backstory with item descriptions, and some of the dialogue.  In DF-9, just about all of the dialogue is tongue-in-cheek, but it succeeds more at confusing the player as to what the character is trying to do than being entertaining, and makes no discernible attempt to flesh out the galaxy.  The same goes for item descriptions, though they can, on occasion, at least give you a little more useful information than the dialogue does.  Character designs are interesting (sometimes), but since alien races don't line up with dialogue or have any impact on a colonist's abilities (just their name) it feels incredibly pointless, and more like the variety is just there because it's what everyone does in sci-fi.

Once you manage to forgive those issues, and actually start playing the game in earnest, you'll get your starting 3 residents.  You build your first handful of rooms of base by assigning them relevant jobs - namely Builder at the start.  Before long, you've got the whole "oxygen" problem under wraps (for the moment anyway), and have enough opportunity to "breathe" to start worrying about and make use of the two major "stat" pages for your residents.  The first, which is much easier to understand the ramifications for, is the Job screen.

When you view all the Jobs for your Base, it's shown as a spreadsheet comparing each resident to each job.  (I find it far more useful than simply viewing one resident and a list of each job.)  There, you get to see which jobs residents like or dislike doing - and how strongly - represented by an emoticon, and how skilled they are at each job, represented by a number of stars.  It's a bit strange that there's very little correlation between skills and likes - real people tend not to loathe things they're really good at, nor remain inept at their greatest passion.  But compared to the other issues in the game, this is pretty easy to forgive.  And frankly, this screen does its job just fine.  It's the second "stat" page for citizens, Personal Needs, that can cause nightmares.

At first glance, it's perfectly reasonable.  Sort of like The Sims, each resident has needs that must be met, and they will automatically go about meeting needs, especially if they're far from satisfied.  So if they're Hungry, they'll go to the Food Replicator and acquire some fabricated sustenance, or if they're not feeling sufficiently Social, they'll go chat in the Pub.  But there at the Pub, you'll find a problem that only gets worse the more you learn about it.  Sometimes, your citizens will get into a fight.  In my experience, this always left a citizen knocked out on the ground, though I felt like if I could just get a citizen in Security to respond fast enough, they could break up the fight before anyone gets badly injured.  Anyway, this can give you a considerable setback, as not only does it hurt Morale (which means they're less likely to work), it means the loser/victim will be out of commission for a while, their recovery will take work from your Doctor(s), and you'll need to have sufficient space in the Medbay.

As you grow your base's population to accomodate its continued expansion, fights will break out in greater frequency, naturally causing you to investigate why they do, and how you can prevent them.  So you take a closer look at the citizens' Needs.  And sure, you find that there's usually a correlation between low Morale and fights.  So you keep the food in the Pub better stocked.  You install more Monitors in the base so the citizens can more easily entertain themselves.  Some citizens weren't having their Duty needs met, but it's because you felt a bit of a crunch, and you had citizens doing Jobs just because it's what they were good at, but not what they liked doing.  So you spend an extra ten minutes at the Jobs screen, to make sure everyone's doing a job they at least like doing, if not love, even if it means some jobs will get done a bit slower while they hone their skills.  And things are good for a while; fewer fights, more productivity, means a happy player.  Maybe at this point you're starting to struggle with the increased frequency of Raider attacks, but for the sake of completing this thought before talking about that one, let's say everything's actually starting to go well.  It's going well, that is, until the citizens start fighting again.

You check the Morale of everyone involved in the fight, and it's doing alright.  The fight may have caused the victim/loser to take a dip in theirs, but it's certainly not what caused it.  Each of the needs is pretty well satisfied.  But then you take a closer look at the aggressor's Needs.  He's been at a job he loves for a while now, and his Duty is well satisfied - fully satisfied, actually.  Everything looks great.  But then you look at his personal job rating - egotistical.  That's right, if you make your citizens too happy, they'll overinflate their egos, and fight each other anyway!  It was at this point I had to put the game down for good.  But this came after I had been struggling with Raiders for many playthroughs.

Apparently I need to keep it short due to review length limits.  Basically, they wind up getting extremely hard as time goes on, seemingly increasing in difficulty faster than you can hope to develop defenses.  There seems to be a sort of "final wave" of Raiders but I was never able to fend them off, even with a dozen point defense lasers shooting down most of their ships.

In summary, think long and hard before deciding to buy Spacebase DF-9.  It's not just not for everyone, it's only for a very niche, forgiving group of gamers.

I am well aware of Tim Schafer's Molyneux-esque decline from a position of respected industry veteran to corporate slime-ball.  I am also well aware of Spacebase DF-9's troubled development and reputation as the quintessential example of a consumer-unfriendly kickstarter failure.

So why did I pick up this game?  It was dirt cheap on sale and, in theory, it contains many elements of a game that I should enjoy.  Base construction, resource and personnel management, quirky characters to enlist or engage- all wrapped up in a sci-fi setting.  I was expecting that it would be an incomplete experience good for a couple of hours of play with no worthwhile end-game.

"Incomplete" doesn't even begin to describe this disaster of a game.  The UI is unintuitive.  The AI is incompetent.  The QA is nonexistent.  Each of these elements adds a layer of frustration to the experience that, had I known existed, I would not have bothered to play even if you payed me the price of the game to do so.  Every element is broken on some level.  Had the developers an ounce of integrity, they could have easily invested the time (for which they had been paid in advance) to bring it to a servicable level, but this is nothing more than an embarrassment for which they should be ashamed.

Do not buy this game.  Do not buy games from this developer... unless it's Psychonauts.  Buy that instead.

Spacebase DF9 is a space management simulator where a small pod of astronauts set out to create a new space colony. You have to manage oxygen, food, jobs and the happiness of your intergalactic residents. As you progress, you will need to continue expanding to make space for new residents. The game had the potential to become an enjoyable simulator, but fell short in so many ways. 

PROS: 
The graphics are decent. 
The sound is fitting for the game. 
Most of the astronauts are not human, they are alien, making for more interesting looking characters. 

CONS: 
The game is very repetitive. After only an hour of gameplay, all the messages are the same, all your residents are saying the same things, everyone behaves the same etc. The game is severely lacking in variety. 
The A.I. is brutally stupid. Your colony can die because your mechanic is to depressed to fix the oxygen generators, killing everyone. 
There is quite a limited amount of things to build. Once you build each type of room, all you can do is keep making the same things as more astronauts arrive. No matter what, the gameplay is boring after the first hour or so. 
There is a lot of waiting, even when you speed things up. 
When you encounter problems, there is a fixed solution to deal with them. It gets even more boring and repetitive when you are forced to do the same steps continuously as the game progresses. 

It all comes down to is repetitiveness and a loss of interest. The game could be so much better if there were more scenarios and problems and multiple unique strategies to use. Unfortunately, this game is not worth the price when there are so many better alternatives available.

[h1] Overview [/h1] 

Spacebase DF-9 is a survival game in the wide-reaching void of, you guessed it, space. Your mission is work with a trio of astronauts and build the most sophisticated, comprehensive and long-lasting space station anyone has ever seen. That sounds amazing on paper, and being developed from the veterans over at Double Fine Productions, you’d almost be assured a great game. However, the product falls short and development has long since died for this title, leaving an ugly mess in its wake. In space, nobody can hear you complain.

The game opens up with an interesting concept at first – a map laid out with all the locations in the galaxy, letting you pick where you want to start and factoring in variables like meteor showers, derelict ships, traffic for earning more crew members [good and bad] and resources. Once your base is selected, you’re launched into space with three crew members, a space pod for power and oddly, no spaceship; the game starts you out in the dead of space with limited oxygen, limited supplies and a very short time span before your whole crew perishes from asphyxiation. From a logical standpoint, the start of the game makes absolutely no sense and it only gets worse from there.

You must quickly build a functioning center with enough life support for your crew. You’ll gather material from nearby asteroids that oddly resemble play-doh, which you will ingeniously craft into oxygen recyclers and stations for power with nothing but a blowtorch and your wits. As the base grows, you’re able to expand, making different rooms that can be retrofitted into housing, laboratories, pubs, infirmaries and more. 

I like the aspect of building a base to my own liking, but Double Fine really chokes the life out of personalizing it as you see fit: limited items to use, each room can only use furniture from one list of items [I.E. only residential furniture in a residence] which forces you to build a lot of unnecessary rooms for no reason at all. However, my biggest complaint is being in space and not being able to build along the Z axis; you can only build outward, not vertically, which seems like a huge oversight since you’re not hindered by the laws of gravity.

As you continue playing, you’ll encounter hazards that you must overcome, such as illness, resource management [marginally], machine repairs, raiders [space pirates] and meteor showers. Most obstacles aren’t all that exciting: meteor showers are not impressive and barely noticeable if the game didn’t tell you it was happening, space pirates have terrible AI capabilities and can easily be killed with a few well-placed defense turrets and most ailments can be cured by simply sending them to the doctor, curing them nearly instantly. Oddly, some of the ailments have auto-cures, such as when I was afflicted with “Space Blindness”, which I was promptly told there was already a cure so I didn’t have to do anything.

The real gem to this travesty is the writing, or the lack of a proper writer. Here’s an example of the type of “communications” you’ll received while in space:

http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=834694128

I felt secondhand embarrassment just reading it. The writing is dreadful, out of place and just downright terrible. Couple that with other gems like my dead astronaut having a “kinda happy” job satisfaction while simultaneously being dead, but the real winner is that her location is “space”:

http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=834702535

Yes, everything in this game has "space" attached to it. Your location, beds are called "space beds" and even rugs are called "space rugs" because your typical Ikea rug is not suitable for the vacuum of space apparently.

I could go on and on with all the issues with this game, but in the end it has been abandoned completely by Double Fine and is left at the hands of 3rd party modders if they feel like investing their time in such a project. Much like my crew member Nashira Corrino, this game is dead, asphyxiated by its own mediocrity. 

[h1] Pros [/h1] 

[list]
[*] There are none.
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1] 

[list] 
[*] The entire game is a con. There are too many to list. The game has been abandoned. Stay away.
[/list]


Overall, Spacebase DF-9 is an absolute mess with broken AI, poor graphics, terrible UI and even worse sound effects. There is literally no reason for you to play this unless you’re punishing yourself and even less reason to buy it unless you’re sending it to someone in hopes of terminating a friendship.

This game gets an 8/10 from me. It's a really relaxing game when taken for what it is. I am reviewing it as version 1.06 Mac OSX no mods installed. I had a free version for months before finding it on steam for 99¢ and just had to buy it to encourage the developers just a little bit with my tiny contribution. I would easily pay $5 bucks for it.

You're basically thrown into space, given 3 guys and very little resources to start building your space base. In the beginning you need to start as small as possible, building just the bare necessities. Once you have a small (3x3) airlock room, another room just large enough to hold 3 oxygen recyclers, and a room just large enough for a matter refinery, the rest is a piece of cake.

The game is 90% relaxing, mining and building, welcoming new (weird & silly) inhabitants, and pretty much trying to keep everyone fed, breathing, and happy - or as happy as one can be in a fragile domicile in space. You need to begin early considering how to protect your base from bad guys that pop in periodically, and asteroid impact damages.

Aside from the few (easy) dangers, it's just a relaxing sandbox style building game where you can be creative in making a space base to be proud of. The interface is pretty much well organized, which is an aspect that many games like this get wrong. I enjoy the weird types of characters/aliens and their thoughts and interactions.

Many people complain about the AI being retarded, but you have to pay attention to what each character is good or bad at and by what degree they would suck at a job. You have to assign them to duties they are good at and actually enjoy doing. Some are good at a job, but hate doing it, so yeah, they'll stand around playing games on their pads instead of doing any work, unless you assign them to a duty they enjoy. I find this aspect completely adorable, as it really adds to the immersion and how you feel or care for each individual. I also love the names - imagining how an alien would pronounce his name written as "Uneekly (nicely)" - that sorta thing.

It's currently (for the past several months) been my favorite game for when I just want to relax and make a creative little space base. The few, easy dangers add just enough of that random aspect to keep you on your toes and influence the shape and direction your base takes. Have lots of good tech guys and your base will run smoothly - put lotsa gun turrets all around the outside walls and you'll be safe enough to survive a large attack that eventually happens. And just have fun building and watching how your inhabitants get along.

My only complaint is - once you get a VERY LARGE base, things go bad fast. Machines start failing, catching on fire, destroying themselves everywhere, no matter how many techs you have to fix them. But I guess this is just a sign that I've gone way too far with this base and should just start a new one, haha.

Lotsa people be hatin' on it, but it's been one of my favorite, relaxing games that I keep going back to.

This game is very screwy. You've been sent deep into the galaxy to help seed the remnants of human civilization throughout space after the fall of Earth. You're not alone, you get help from nearby strangers in similar situations. You never get to actually take control of anything though, the people do whatever they want and all you can do it provide some guidance. More often than not, succeeding involves less strategy and skill, but simply getting lucky.

With that said, I've been having fun with it. There isn't a whole lot to the game. I really wish they would finish it, or perhaps publish it open source so we could develope it further, because it has enormous potential to be an exceptionally entertaining experience.

If you get it, you're going to notice a few problems right away. There are almost no settings. I think you can basically turn the sound on or off and that's it. The game's artwork is quite simplistic and usually runs smoothly, but the HUD menues are overloaded with special effects and animations that will make your framerate drop to crap any time they open. Once you've done the tutorial level and are ready to actually play the game, you may spend more time just looking for a decent place on the galaxy map to build your base than the time you spend actually getting to play. The whole game then gets quite confounded by the mood mechanics. While there are things you can do to help people be happier, and I've had lots of happy folks in some of my bases, they all inevitably gravitate towards depression and then stop working and everything goes to crap and the oxygen runs out and they all suffocate.

Once you get to that point, you discover that there is no way to actually loose the game! Even with everyone dead and your base in ruins, you can still get new people on random chance and continue playing, even though they are almost certainly doomed.

The whole game is wacky that way. It makes a whole lot of no sense. But, still, it's fun, somehow. As long as you don't think abut it too hard or take it too seriously, building one base after another while being hounded by pirates and metoeor showers and ocasionally having some suicidal idiot walk out the wrong door and drift away into space can be pleasantly amusing. This is a game you can just relax with and generally expect to fail at every time you play.

Unfortunately, Gormlessness is clearly contagious as our superhero stepped out of the airlock, went into a panic himself, rushed back into the airlock and flushed himself into space...

I'm sure everyone knows this, but I must include it on my review. This game has been abandoned by the developers.

The developers are also expecting modders to finish the game for them...but didn't make a workshop compatability...*facepalm*. Seriously devs? so at the moment, there are very few mods out there and they are scattered all over the internet, and google search is no help. 

However, there is a new mod called "unoffical patch" to fix some bugs and add some features. I recommend you download that mod or be greeted with bugs apocalypse. 

Now lets talk gameplay.

I don't know what they normally call them, settlers? austronaut? pawn? I'll just name it "people".
Unfortunately, you can't move your people, which can be very annoying when raiders are on sight.
You can assign them up to 9 jobs, some people are more skilled on certain job and also enjoy/hate certain job.
The jobs are;
Builder: self explanatory 
Technician: maintain and fixes objects
Miner: self explanatory
Security: shoot hostile enemy, and follow security beacon that you can set.
Bartender: Tends the bar which increase happiness.
Botanist: tends the garden.
Scientist: Make researches to unlock things.
Doctor: Heal and cure diseases/illness
Janitor: Clean corpses
Unassigned: default

People have needs, and they can go up and down shown on a graph. I don't know what most of these does to the person.
Duty, Social, Morale, Stuff, Energy, Hunger, Fun. Those are the 7 needs of a person.

People also have "thoughts" that you can read. Some of them are about friends and enemy they made, an object they built, or even a certain doom they are about to encounter. Thoughts really define them and I enjoy pausing the game and reading them. 
They also have a nice hand drawn avatar so you know what they look like and perks, if they have low self esteem or they are anxious, etc.

Each person really is different from the rest and it's amazing how much detail they have. It's ashamed this game is abandoned.

Now let's talk about building.
There are 13 rooms you can build, and they are;
Airlock: In and out of the space station
Life Support: For placing Oxygen machine 
Reactor: for powering the entire space station
Refinery: smelting rocks into matter (money)
Residence: Build beds to increase population limit
Pub: increase happiness
Garden: Grow food
Fitness: gym
Research: build research table for scientist
Infirmary: Hospital
Brig: prison
Command: Threat monitoring
Unzoned: plain old room 
Each of these rooms have certain objects that can only be placed on that room. All objects (and wall/floor) cost matter to build.
Matter can be obtained by mining rocks and smelting it on a refinery machine. 

To build a room, you need to inclosed it with walls and floors. If a wall or a floor is destroyed, and a person is in that room, they will be sucked into the vacume of space and die.
Walls/floors and objects can be destroyed from astroids and raiders. 

There are random encounter in the game.
There are people that you can communicate with that randomly pops up (when they are near you).
If you respond to their message, then you can either gain a person or be targeted by raiders.
This is the risk you need to think about before accepting their calls.
There are also an actual spaceship that shows in your game. You can either send your security (via security beacon) or leave it alone until it leaves the game. 

Spacebase DF9 had potentials, but its been abandon before it can even fly. I really wish someone would make a similar game. SOMEONE PLEASE! 

That being said, would I recommend this game? Not on full price. Buy this game when it's 90% on sale.

First up, I will say that I have personally enjoyed playing it overall, despite the many gripes I have. However, the sheer quantity of gripes means I simply cannot in good conscience recommend the game to others.

To put it simply, the game is really, really hard, because the AI is awful and the game hardly gives you a chance to recover from one raider attack to the next. I literally end up with 10s of bodies littered around the inside and outside of the space-station because the medical staff (who are supposed to clean these bodies up) do so at a slower rate than new bodies are generated. Your station crew love attacking eachother due to unhappiness, with no obvious way of resolving their unhappiness. Your non-security personnel love to run directly into the line of fire of the raider boarding party, whilst your actual security personnel will slowly amble over from the other end of the base, even though you put down a beacon more than 30 seconds ago. 

However, the fact the game is hard due to the rubbish AI is, I think, what makes me enjoy it. I can build a successful space-station despite the crew being my worst enemy.

The game also, in general, feels unfinished - which is probably not surprising because, despite what Double Fine Productions may tell you, it simply isn't. They basically cancelled the game and released a Version "1.0" which did tidy up some loose ends but by no means all of them, nor did it add any sorely-needed late-game content.

Whilst the game itself is very buggy, when you use the unofficial patch (http://www.spacebasehub.net/download/) the game runs perfectly fine. So my review is based purely on the game with the patch, as it is thoroughly enjoyable. 
Also, 69p for a game wthat you have to use a community made patch to be enjoyable is totally fine by me.

Dissapointing....  Back when the game was in early development I fell victim to its "appeal".  I saw a game with potential and I was all and all hopeful.  In those ealier days the game was riddled with bugs and glitches, and when I found out they were dropping the game and rushing development, I was hopeful they would eliminate those bugs and glitches in the game.  So as a review of the official release of version 1.06 here is the breakdown.  I'll have a simple review and more in depth... or in this game... anger driven review...

----- Simple ----

The game is crap... It had so much potential but since it got the axe and a speedy release... it has so many issues.  I honestly tried to play the game again... but yet I wasn't able to play longer than 10 minues.  I would not recommend this game to anybody unless it's less than a dollar or given to you free.  It's buggy... rough to control, and just honestly crap.

----- Angered Version -----

Graphics:
As this is not a "Highly graphical" game I wouls say they are acceptable.  The sprites perform actions that is befiting, and nothing to standoutish.  However in aspect of gameplay the "isometric" angle makes the game difficult to know exactly what is going on.  In the typical fashion the walls disappear in a way to allow you to see in the rooms, however being able to roatate the camera would be nice.

Gameplay:
This is where the game loses me.  Although the controls aren't "hard" they are difficult in there own way.  I've played many builder games, and most games play similarily with minor adjustments to the controls.  In more recent terms since the era of shooter games almost every game depends upon the W-A-S-D model.  This game doesn't stray too far fram that idea and it feels comfortable... at least until you start building.  At that point the game takes a turn for the worst.  Edge scrolling doesn't feel like it's in existence, so your dependant upon the WASD model, but once you open the construction menu, foul language fills the mouth as when you click with your mouse to select the item and press "D" to move your contruction item changes.  As soon as that construction menu comes up the game shifts from a comfortable WASD model to a point and click model.  This wouldn't be a problem if they didn't establish you could use the WASD in the first place....   So that is annoying.  Then it gets worse.  As you play you decide to speed up the game, and most games using some button near the WASD (tab, 123, something) changes the game speed, but in comes the mouse model, and you have to click the speed options.  Now I wouldn't have an issue with this, if it wasn't for the fact that when any ship arrived or any notification appears the game switches back to speed 1.... and DOES NOT RETURN.....I find it quite annoying because I'll be in the middle of waiting for my characters to build a room... then all the sudden a message... then the question, "Why are my guys moving so slow"... then oh gotta click that speed... then the game goes NOPE... and another message.  It just continually pesteres you until you get so angry that you give up.

AI:
I don't normally judge AI as it's always an issue with all games.  It is always about finding that right balance between what the computer needs to process and what the character prioritizes.... unfortunately it appears that this game said, "F*$k it... have the guys do whatever."  And like loyal programs they do whatever.  You have absolutely no control over the individual character, so when your trying to finish that bed... your have to wait until the game decides... "know what I think I should build that bed."  But at that point your characters are now falling over because they are so tired... that they have no energy... then get depressed and not want to work... so now that bed will never get done.... it annoying the bleeping crap out of me as I was just trying to enjoy the game.

Glitches and Bugs:
Yes I'm bringing it up... as a "fully" released game you would expect most of the bugs and glitches to be taken care of... in fact thats what most of the follow up forums established... but know what.... turns out that your characters get stuck (dumb AI) and because you can't do that they sufficate.... yeah... so just started finished the basic build... airlock... air... and such... but oh no... two of my guys just sat there... doing... NOTHING... could it be AI? probably... but to me that's a bug.   But it's not the worst oh no... in my honest to goodness no opinion try I got "invaded" another ship attached itself to me, and I was assulted.  After killing the AI I noticed, Hey there is a gun outside...  Then I slowly watched one of my security guards go out to take care of it.... two shots later dead.... ok..... so what does the AI do?  "Well he's dead... probably should take care of that... but naa...."  Guess where my miners had to go to get resources?  Right in the line of fire.... so there goes two of my miners...  Well maybe I can control a security... oh wait can't control the guys so whoops... maybe set a security point for them.... nope... dead... dead and dead.....  I'm happy they incorperated the guns for defences... but when a gun is established as enemy and even if you took over everything it appears that that guns still acts hostile....  My frustrations knows no bounds.

Overall the game is fine.... just fine.... not great... not good... just fine.... if you want something new to distract you for 10 minutes... here is the perfect game for you... but don't buy unless it's on uber sale.... and by uber sale like... I dunno $0.99 per copy... or heck maybe if the company pays you to play... becuase honestly this game isn't worth anything more.

This one's a little tough, because I really wanted to like this game. I'm a fan of survival games and sims (both with and without capital-S). Spacebase DF9 has a nice idea and a rather decent realisation. The gameplay is all right, and the design, particularly of the inhabitants of the space station, is pretty cool. BUT. The game has been abandoned by the devs and currently relies on community patches to work. Don't expect any fixes for the bugs that are still in the game.

What is there is the groundwork for the Sims in space. Sort of. You're starting out with three astronauts and a small amount of resources, just enough to build a closed space to shelter your little aliens from, well, actual space. From there, you mine resources, add to your space station room by room, and slowly develop a complex microcosmos that has you manage life-sustaining installations like reactors and oxygen generators, necessities like food dispensers, a medical bay and bedrooms, and luxuries like a bar and a fitness room. Additional challenges include raids and abandoned drifting space stations to discover and loot to your heart's content.

But that's where the content ends. It's a very bare-bones game that gets repetitive fast. The AI is borderline stupid as soon as something goes wrong, with people running around screaming at the tiniest fire instead of using the extinguishers and subsequently letting the entire station burn, others starving to death because the food dispenser was too far away (in the next room), and the doctor preferring to eat five times in a row at said food dispenser instead of incinerating the bodies of those who died in the last pirate raid - who have only died because security idled at the opposite end of the station until I specifically directed them to fight the raiders. You have to micromanage everything, because you can't trust the AI. Even after you assign jobs to people, they will sometimes refuse to do them, even if it's their preferred occupation. Security officers will not intervene unless you tell them to, and then one at a time, getting killed by absurdly overpowered raiders.
Who will always show up as soon as your station hits a certain number of people (ridiculously low, six, if I remember right), and will start out super-strong. Contrary to what the "map" selection suggests, there is no way to adjust the difficulty unless you change the game files manually, and even then it often doesn't work. The area of space that you pick has no tangible impact on how hard the game is; the number of raiders and meteor strikes seems consistent across the board, the only thing that changes is how often empty stations drift by yours.
It's crazy hard to survive after hitting the threshold after which raiders spawn, and borderline impossible once you've reached ten and higher because the game keeps spawning higher and higher numbers of enemies, forcing you to assign around half of your inhabitants to security. That, in turn, prevents you from playing a lot of the other features, like botany, which you need for the bar, or science, which you need for almost all upgrades. The balance is shoddy, and Double Fine did not bother to fix it, instead abandoning the game.
Fans have stepped in and created one (to my knowledge, so far) patch to fix a few of these bugs, but there is no guarantee it'll work with your game. And it shouldn't have to, if DF didn't stop working on games once it becomes too much work. It seems like the game didn't sell as many copies as they anticipated, and they decided it wasn't worth the effort, instead starting another crowdfunding campaign for a new game. That looks like a really shady business practice, like you'd find on the seedier side of Greenlight and Early Access, and one I can't support.

Being a fan of the old “Tycoon” games and “Theme Hospital” I was really excited about Space Base DF-9. I thought for sure reviewers were being too hard on it, so as soon as I saw it pop up in a Humble Bundle I was ecstatic… But, all of my excitement was for naught. Almost 6 hours wasted and I can pretty well guarantee I will never touch this title again.

[b][u]TL;DR [/u][/b]
There is a ton of promise here. When the game is running smooth there’s not a lot to complain about (except maybe lack of construction options), but eventually that smooth ride will be over and you’ll realize nothing works like it should, if at all. So while playable you’ll hit a point where the effort to advance isn’t worth it. If you still think you want to punish yourself by playing this game make sure you check out http://www.spacebasehub.net/ for the unofficial patch, the mechanics are still broken but everything else has been improved.

[b][u]In-depth Review[/u][/b]
[b]Overall Gameplay: [/b]
The basic construction and management section of the game is fairly well done. It’s very similar to “Theme Hospital”, but with a slightly improved interface. That’s where the positives end. So many things are broken that it becomes unnecessarily difficult, and not in a fun, challenging way but in a “oh there’s another thing that doesn’t work right” kind of way. 
Here are just a few examples of things you’ll see characters do:
- Die of suffocation despite being surrounded by rooms with oxygen and having access to an airlock with space suits, 
- Become incapacitated (not dead, just lying around uselessly) indefinitely. If they’re Raiders they actually might be back up and start killing people!
- Be marked for the brig or infirmary but never go there
- Scientists not researching (despite being assigned research and having a research station).
- Ignore the 3 fire extinguishers near the fire, and instead stomp on it until they catch on fire, then run around the base being ignored by everyone else until they burn to death… Actually that might’ve been the most entertaining part of the game!

[b]Presentation:[/b] 
The user interface is easy to navigate but overly simple. You only have 1 save slot and the game auto saves by default, so if you’re not careful it’s quite easy to erase a save game by clicking on the wrong thing and not exiting before it overwrites your game.

The graphics are fine. They’re quite obviously a throwback to “Theme Hospital” (how many times can I name dop?). It works well for the genre, and they’re fairly sharp. 

The sound is outright boring, the music is nothing impressive and off the top of my head I honestly don’t remember any sounds other than that and the chirping alarm if you zoom in far enough.


[b][u]Summary:[/u][/b]
This game could be so good, but as in so many cases now it looks like the developer took their money and ran. In my love/hate relationship with Early Access this is why the hate portion exists. I’d give it a 3/10, it’s playable and as long as things work right it’s quite enjoyable, but the unpredictable and frustrating broken mechanics make it another EA Trash title. Pick it up in a bundle with some good games or for $1 or less and get a couple hours of fun… But DO NOT, under any circumstances pay any more for it than that. Especially when you could get the vastly superior Theme Hospital and forget this all together.

Spacebase DF-9 lets you create your own space station, managing crew and resources all while staving off pirates and taking hails. It sounds like a lot of fun for anyone that was into Star Trek or even games like Dungeon Keeper 2, but it turns into all of the management and none of the fun. The big issues that I have with the game is that its tough to survive the first few moments of a normal game and beyond that, its just a dull game that forces you to assimilate all metal to keep growing your station to accommodate more crew.

Your objective is to keep your crew alive against first asphyxiation and later raiders. Even when your crew dies and the game tells you start a new game, it still continues. It is a game over without being concrete or giving you a final score before you have to start a new game.

To start with, there's an optional easy how to play tutorial level that will guide you through the basics without feeling forced upon you. The tutorial makes it easy to get up and running. Assign crew to the roster of jobs. Builders build when you construct rooms or objects. Miners will mine ore to be refined to get more matter to construct with. Technicians fix things and that's about as far as the tutorial gets.

You'll need a few things to get a space base operational. The first is power that comes in the form of reactors or a seed to start with. The second is the base itself which can be a giant room. You'll need an oxygen recycler since you are in space after all. After your space base has O2, an enclosed room and power, there's another matter and that's getting in. To do this you need to setup an air lock with two airlock doors one to the interior and the other to the exterior. This room also needs to have a locker for space suits.

Outside of the tutorial the giant problem that I have with the game is the level of difficulty when you're even getting started. The tutorial is nice and setup and it does let you continue on playing which is perhaps the best method. Consider that easy mode. You get to select your location and the game tells you how rich in ore and the frequency of attacks. Its a nice choice of difficulty without being a blunt difficulty slider.

In normal play, the game starts you with a seed for power and three crew in space suits with limited oxygen. There is so much that can go wrong. Running out of matter before your crew is in oxygen will doom you. So you need to budget building a small room to house the seed, a recycler, food dispenser, and a second for the air lock. Then you need to wait for the station to fill with oxygen and even for the air lock to cycle air in and out. Your spacemen can die in their suits when waiting for an air lock to pressurize. Oh but there is another nail to get caught on and that's the fact ore needs to be converted into matter, so it requires a matter refinery. This getting started kicks off the game and it will scare people away.

On paper, interesting things do happen. Derelict space stations will come into your area for you to explore and spaceships will dock with you. From there you have a choice, send your security over to investigate them or ignore them. The spaceships become part of your base where then you need to claim each room, which can be tedious and cumbersome since many small rooms are just tough to click on.

People can come aboard infected with a disease and then your science station will be put to work finding the cure. To do so, click whatever science room you've setup and select whatever they should research. There are a number of diseases to cure and upgrades to unlock. Upgrades include things like body armor and heavier doors.

You will get attacked from time to time. Raiders will float out in space and either try to shoot your miners as they pass by or they will board your station. Other times vessels will dock with your station and you'll be invaded. The catch is, unless you're watching a mining operation, its easy to spot and prepare for. You can have your security waiting for them, unless they're busy putting out a fire. It seems like more of an annoyance than a fun or cool challenge. You can also purchase wall mounted defense turrets.

Normal crew will still engage the enemy if they're in the same room, but to send crew in to fight hostiles, you'll need to assign crew to the security. From there you can make a security beacon that draws them to the area. It feels like an extra step and even marking the point and calling off security seems like it could be streamlined. A lot of the game needs to be streamlined.

Once attackers are incapacitated you can act to cuff, uncuff or execute them. In fact you can chose to execute or cuff any of your crew. Its just a little odd. Sometimes they will even chose to join your crew. Once resources become scarce, its just easier to execute them and dump them into the refiners to make matter.

Sometimes there is an issue where a firefight in an airlock can down the only crew inside the station. So anyone outside the station is forced to suffocate over time because the air lock refuses to open when someone is in there without a suit. It gets more hilarious because in smaller stations, crew will just stand in the air lock when its too crowded everywhere else. Spacebase DF-9 is an amazing game to watch because of its logic.

Speaking of logic, I managed to glitch the game into thinking there was no airlock. Those outside the station would die of asphyxiation and those inside the station would stay in there. Even crew joining would stay outside until they died. Destroying the airlock doors and rebuilding had no effect. Yet I could manually keep a door open so the spacemen could float into my base still in their suits. They would still suffer the same fate with no oxygen. The only way I was able to get people in and out was to build a new airlock.

In terms of crew management, when it comes to the roster everyone has an emotion to specific jobs no matter what their skill level is. You can have someone great at botany, yet hates doing it. Crew member you're the best doctor we have! Yeah but they get sad while doing it. Its a realistic and offers a level of micro management. Once you get to a point where you have crew of every class it gets easier since you no longer have people flip jobs such as having a miner one day and builder the next.

You get constant hails to answer and decide if you want them to join. It feels like a chore so I opt to avoid the calls. Sometimes the hails are to lull you into security so they can get "in your base, killing your dudes." Their transmissions all seems sketchy. There is no one that sounds like a clear cut good or bad choice. They all sound like they're trying to be funny and questionable, because that's what people like in their games, humor and charm. Well both fall flat and it feels forced.

Its also annoying having to press the faster speed setting, because the game will drop to normal speed whenever a yellow notice appears. It could be worse by being a popup box that you have to click like in so many other games. These warnings are things such as a crew member is starving or running out of oxygen. These warnings are color coated. Green means an overall hint on what's needed in your station such as more self space. Yellow and brown seem to be specific crew have achieved something or need something. Major warnings like crew being attacked or raiders about to board are in yellow so they blend in. A lot of times I realize we've been attacked after I see the number of crew go down. Raiders look similar to your own crew.

Spacebase DF-9 is just a tough game to love when it feels like a tough start followed by dull and uninspired management. It does feel like a fleshed out game with a lot of annoyances. I think scenarios would help extend my interest, but within a few hours I feel like I've seen everything there is to see. With all of that said, it is still worth the one dollar I paid for it.

[b][i]Spacebase DF-9[/i][/b] is a casual building sim-tycoon game. You are put in charge of a few colonists to build, maintain and protect your own space station.

[b]Pros[/b]: The game is easy to pick up on: you start with a power source, minerals and a handful of colonists whose first priority is to build a modest space station with oxygen supplies, and expand to a small variety of room types while mining and refining minerals. As your crew grows and time passes, additional needs will surface, needs that you must address or risk your crew to lose its temper. Derelict ships and additional travelers will want to join, some whether you like it or not, and you must deal with meteor showers, raiders and other threats, all the while researching better equipment.

[b]Cons[/b]: There is a severe lack of variety in every way: Only a couple of room types with very little content or options, while general furniture offers a scarce selection. Travelers will often discard your rejection, and you quickly become over-populated. You barely have any control over crew morale. The game become repetitive as you are constantly facing the same issues: need more resource or oxygen/power, raiders come over to kill some of your crew, crew member goes berserk, rinse & repeat. Even tech research is rather limited.

[b]Verdict[/b]: ★★☆☆☆ - Forget it

[i]Spacebase DF-9[/I] drops the ball. While not a bad game, it had the potential of being the next [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/297920/][i]Space Colony[/i][/url], but doesn't come even close. Games of this genre require variety to make it interesting to build and grow, and this game doesn't have what it takes to give it the replay value it would need.

As far as abandon titles go, this one seems like it is close to being complete. However, two big elements are missing. 

First, there is gameplay balance. The game starts off feeling like you can do anything in it, if you just put the time and effort into it. And for the first 20 or 30 minutes this feels true.  You expand your base, explore ships, and manage your people to get the most out of them.  But then the raiders, and meteor strikes happen. And this is where the missing gameplay balance is most obvious.  Negative events are important to any game, if things were always good, than there wouldn't be any challenge. But the speed, and frequency of the negative events needs to be balance out against what the play can and cannot do, so that they can overcome them, and not just suffer.  I found that during the few games that I played, that I would get close to having a decent base going, only to have ruin by constant attacks, to the point where I was losing a lot more people than I was generating. Which resulted in me having a large empty base that I had no chance of defending or using.

The second element is content. There isn't much in this game... 

Overall, this is not a game that you should spend money or time in.

Ok, so this game.  Great concept.  Great idea, and it is done really well.  Except for one main thing.  The game constantly throws stuff at you, and sometimes there isn't actually a good answer.  Let me explain.  You are building a big section of your base.  Things are going well.  You then see a message appear on the side of the screen saying how one of your builder's space suit oxygen is running low.  Sometimes they quickly make their own way back to the airlock, stopping them from dieing.  Sometimes they just carry on working and then die.  You can try to avoid this by sending them to the infirmary (which is obviously inside) manually.  But sometimes they don't bother to listen and still die.

  Another example of this game throwing rubbish into your face would be those raiders who have high tech weaponry.  It takes one of them to take out tonnes of vital parts to your station as well as many many people with inferior weaponry, and thats it.  Your space base is broken and/or on fire and half your population dead.  Yay.

The random space debris causing major fires and ruptures within your base can easily kill a room full of sleeping people, again almost half your bases population. 

But the main thing that gets me is that for a game that is meant to be a mix between economy and fighting, all the fighting is unfair (see the first paragraph) and the economy lacks whats really needed.  The AI don't know when to prioritise fixing vital oxygen recyclers over fixing an unused door.  They also don't know when it is useful to take a break - many will take a break and not perform tasks during critical points in gameplay, causing negative effects (most prominently the players mood).  

In conclusion this game has a lot of potential.  A lot.  But it doesn't have basic concepts like manual prioritization and decent AI.  The whole game needs a huge amount of balancing, and until this happens I recommend you simply follow this game, rather than get it.  If and when the devs make the changes necessary this game will definately worth the money.  But for now, I recommend you spend it elsewhere.

And one other thing.  I can't for the life of me find out a way of keeping the people happy.  It may just be my incompetance, or this too may need balancing...

The developer abandoned it because, as far as I can tell, they just plain didn't think it was selling well enough to be worth putting money into finishing the game.  It's kind of crushing that a company that had a positive reputation like DoubleFine would just abandon a half-made game like this.  (And for the record, my first real notification of this was that my previous positive early-access review managed to get a near-constant stream of downvotes for the simple fact that it had been a positive review...)  The "consolation prize" was that they handed out free Hack 'n' Slash games to purchasers of this game (limited time, already over), although it raises the question of why players would trust in the next early access game when the last one was abandoned...

That said, I don't have the same bitterness a lot of people seemed to have. (Likely because I don't live in hype of upcoming games when I'm sitting on a mountain of Steam games I've got in reserve.)  

As for the game, itself, it's fairly simple.  Start with nothing but a few resources, build an airlock and air recycler quick to not suffocate when your suits run out of air, build a mining station, and start mining for more resources.  From there, use resources to start making more rooms, and stuffing them full of all the random things in the menu until you have a little of everything.  Then have random visitors stay at your station, and start building MORE of everything.  Then have asteroids slam into your station (just lock everyone out of the threatened rooms), or have some raiders (set everyone to security, and bum rush them all), or have other mystery stations drift nearby (remove their walls from the outside to suck all the likely hostile inhabitants into the vacuum of space instead of letting your guys get killed). By and large, the game just lather, rinses, and repeats from there.  

If you really like managers, I can say you might have fun with it for a few hours, but don't get it unless it's absolutely dirt cheap, because you're probably going to experience everything this game really has to offer in about 6 hours or so, and from there, it's just a matter of building a base larger and larger to cram more and more population in.
