Spacebase DF9’s 2,859 “mostly negative” reviews (at the time of writing) are probably more a testament to Steam’s ubiquity as a content delivery tool than to the game’s own (very real) problems. And it does have problems, to be sure, but depending on your outlook and how much you pay for it, they’re not insurmountable.

Its gameplay appears at first to be something along the lines of the legendary Dwarf Fortress, Mucky Foot’s 2001 classic Startopia, or Firefly Studios’  2003 Space Colony, but its flaws – the result of a suddenly-abandoned development process – make it play more like a Roguelike. Your rather nebulous goal is to re-populate the galaxy by building endless space stations, staffing them with an ever-increasing supply of wandering space travellers and keeping them happy and safe from weird diseases, bloodthirsty raiders and each other. Material for building comes from mining asteroids or disassembling passing wrecks and derelicts, and your rooms and corridors are built and then assigned different uses – residential, life support, various social, scientific and utilitarian functions. There’s a strong people-management aspect too, as each new arrival at your base can be assigned to one of eight different duties, each of which will make them feel varying degrees of satisfaction or frustration, and each of which they’ll be good or bad at according to a 1-5 star system. In all respects, the UI is super friendly and makes juggling your people as easy as possible. Which is great, because you can eventually build gigantic structures with literally dozens and dozens and dozens of crewmembers. Crucially though, you have almost zero direct control over your people. You can only order them to report to the infirmary if they’re injured, and even then it may take them a while to limp their way over.

At first, as you learn the ropes, each new game comes hard and fast. Death comes as a result of being ill-prepared to research a disease cure, or not having sufficient defences against a surprise Raider attack, or for any one of dozens of interestingly unfortunate and unforeseeable reasons (usually often as funny as they are frustrating). But the actual process of making your space stations is so much fun that the urge to immediately try again keeps you clicking, again and again, learning more and more each time, developing and abandoning new ideas and strategies as you go. Spacebase DF 9 is very much one of those Civ/Morrowind-type games that suck the hours out of your life without you realising. Be prepared for some really late nights if you decide to have ‘just one quick go’ before bedtime.

Adding to this feeling is the game’s own save system, which by default consists of toggle-able silent autosaves and a Save and Quit menu option. Like a psychopathic lover, Spacebase DF9 doesn’t want you to be anywhere other than inside it, grinding at full speed. Played like this, the feeling is very much of a  Roguelike’s ‘one life, one death’ trip, and all of this helps mitigate the pain of being screwed by one of the game’s terrible bugs or imbalances.

Yes, they are quite terrible, unfortunately. But in the twenty hours that I’ve played it so far, the problems have been all about imbalance and lack of tweaking, rather than outright bugs. One of the worst of these is the fact that the guns on enemy ships, once they’ve boarded you, remain ‘hostile’ even after you’ve killed or captured the invaders (sometimes they can even be reformed and will join your crew to start a new life), or claimed their ship as your own. Only by eventually disassembling enough of the enemy ship will you be able to cut off power to the gun, thus making it safe. But getting to the bloody thing can be a real game-breaker – these defensive turrets have great range and cut through people in spacesuits like a lightsabre through yogurt. It’s at times like these that the lack of direct control over your spacemen becomes a real tooth-grinder, and you can end up with piles and piles of floating corpses made up of the Builders who foolishly crossed in front of the guns to get behind them (in space, the AI paths in direct lines from point-to-point), as well as the Doctors who went to retrieve their corpses. 

As far as imbalance in the invisible numbers, the worst offender is the near-constant brawling that goes on. At best this leads to a trip to the brig to cool off for the aggressor and a trip to the infirmary for the victim. At worst, guns will be drawn, and people and facilities start falling. In-fighting is a result of a brilliant system of cabin fever that is determined by various things, including job satisfaction and a host of actual personal feelings and emotions, all of which can be monitored on the crew’s individual profiles. Assigning two people who hate each other to a double cabin is a recipe for disaster, while the sight of bloody corpses littering the place has an obvious impact on depression (especially if the deceased was someone’s friend). But again, due to the abruptly aborted development process, it’s one of several crucial, glaringly imbalanced systems. Which, unless Double Fine release the source code, as they’ve promised to but still not yet done, may never be properly sorted out. This is doubly frustrating because a lua-based modding system is present and correct, but so far nobody’s done anything with it.

Like the similarly blighted and similarly great fun Aliens: Colonial Marines, it’s a game with a bad reputation that in reality is only partially deserved. Early adopters and those who saw the potential for a Dwarf Fortress in space have every right to be annoyed (and to make those thousands of “negative” Steam reviews). But for those of us coming to the game in its ‘finished’ state, and aware of the lingering problems, there is still much fun to be had. Double Fine’s original plan for the game was hugely ambitious, ultimately requiring much more funding than they could successfully raise for it (hence the truncated development). It was only unfortunate that they had already taken it well into the Early Access phase at USD 20 a pop before they realised this. But that’s one of the risks of public alphas, crowdfunding and transparent game development. Like condoms, no one's happy when they go wrong. 

If we’re looking at it in financial terms, then in my case I bought it in the 2015 Steam summer sale at -50%, or EUR 4.99, and have played it now for nearly 21 hours. My feeling is that I’ve had at least 20 Euros of fun from it, and that’s quite important. With some AAA titles costing nearly 60 Euro-dollarpounds and offering dozens of hours of gameplay, but failing to deliver even half as much fun, for a flawed gem like Spacebase DF9 to give you that elusive feeling of true, full-belly satisfaction is, I think, quite a feat.

[h1]The first 'promising' Early Access game[/h1]
Double Fine had [url=https://archive.is/irRiB]lot's of plans[/url] for Spacebase DF-9. The game those plans outlined would be [b]well[/b] worth the $20€ price.
As development continued however, more and more of those plans [url=https://archive.is/RBCBP]were laid to rest[/url] and in the end a very select few were ever realized. As such, the game as it stands, is just nowhere close to being worth the price, and should've been priced more like Hack'n'Slash, the game it's being bundled with now, is priced.

Spacebase DF-9 is a perfect example of a phenomenon that continues to this day: wholly unfinished but 'promising' alphas on Early Access.
As Steam's own documentation states, both developers and customers should treat Early Access games as they are know, not as what they might one day become. Devs shouldn't sell promises, and customers shouldn't buy them. But alas, here we are.

I regret buying into Double Fine's promises during Early Access. Because of the few genuinely good games they've put out, it's easy to forget Double Fine's catalogue is more '[i]miss[/i]' than '[i]hit[/i]', Spacebase DF-9 being a prime example of that fact.

[h1]Bottom line[/h1]
Only buy Spacebase DF-9 if you want to support Double Fine. Even then, it might be better to just buy a DF t-shirt or something, rather than to inflate the sales numbers of this mediocre dissapointment.

While there are still many issues in Spacebase DF-9(such as bugs, outdated graphics, and so on), despite the years of production and work, I understand that this is still an incomplete product. Therefore I am not reviewing this game as a complete product, but rather I am reviewing its creative process. As a building management and construction simulator, Spacebase DF-9 fails the most important criterion in any simulation, uniqueness. Uniqueness is a core aspect in simulation games because it is there in which specialties and creativity come together to make an enjoyable and memorable simulation game. Examples of popular simulation games are Goat Simulator, The Sims, and Train Simulator, which all can be easily identified by each of their unique points. That being said, it is hard to find unique points in Spacebase DF-9. As I am writing this review, in trying to remember things that were unique I find myself fixated more on the bugs than actual gameplay. 

Overlooking the bugs, let me break down the gameplay. You build a base, gather resources, and make the base bigger and repeat. You have raiders that attack your base but they don’t present a threat if you properly maintain security. You have asteroid showers that happen every once in a while that start fires and destroy structures such as walls and they need to be patched up. You will get transmissions every once in a while so that people can move in, attack, or attach themselves to the base. The difficulty ramps up as your base becomes larger and more populated; you have to keep track of people’s morale, energy consumption, and security.  That is about it. 

As I have stated earlier, it lacks uniqueness. The simulation itself is very basic and there seems to be a large amount of creative work in creating the characters. Unfortunately, the programmers made the characters expandable, having them die very easily and having a lot of them makes the characters feel insignificant and therefore, their uniqueness insignificant. As a simulation, this game will not stand out in sales or reviews unless the creative department decides to do some major reworking. Furthermore if unchanged and published, this game will stand out as one of many examples of morale hazard in pre-release gaming. 

 [u] Note:[/u] As I was about to post this I realized that this game was published a year ago. I could not fathom that a game this unpolished and lacking in content could be deemed complete by anyone who took pride in their work. In the end, it seems that DoubleFine just took everyone’s money and fled.

DF-9 does not hold up to its promise. Not by a long shot.

Most prominently the power system. Without an actual power meter (like we have for O2) your base will just suddenly lose power if you've built too much. You have no useful way of knowing when to build another reactor. The devs expect you to hover your mouse over each and every room and sum up the power consumption in your head each time you want to take inventory.

Next up is the "story" of the game. One of the last versions must have shoehorned this in because I don't remember it from Alpha5. Basically at some point the game will spontaneously throw multiple raider ships and raider astronauts at you in bulk. I've you've managed to build your base accordingly by then: congratulations for figuring out the simple and boring strategy needed. If you haven't? Well, you can start all over again.

Then as you continue to play and expand your base to meet the other goals you'll notice how the game becomes increasingly glitchy.

And speaking of goals: The "build all the things" goal isn't even possible. I tried. I built everything there is and allegedly I'm still missing something.

Tim Schaefer himself gave the order to pull the plug on development, claiming that not enough people bought the game during Early Access to fund the development. That's right, the business "plan" was to use Early Access money to fund the actual game (smacks head).

Going against most of the people here, it seems, I think DF-9 should get a generally positive review.

So you know where my view comes from: I bought this game early in alpha because I had a DF coupon, but I rarely play early EA games.  Aside from a quick try in alpha, I have only played the current 1.06.  I also rarely look in the forums, so perhaps I'm less angry than some.  :)

Bottom line: if you enjoy city/base/island-building sandbox games, you will enjoy this.

I found exploring the game after a minimal tutorial enjoyable.  I had several false-starts and refined my base layout as I went.  Lost one decent early base when I learned the difference between tear down and vaporize: when removing a section of wall, vaporize removes everything including the floor.  Everybody was blown out before it could be repaired.

The graphics and animation quality are quite nice as are most of the sound effects.  The user interface is also easy to use in most cases.  It has a few issues when it comes to placing objects, especially ones that go on walls.  Even though they might be hard to see sometimes, the game does not allow you to use the south-east and -west walls interior (hidden) side for object placement.  Turrets are one of the few items that can face in any direction and it can be difficult to place the turrent as it will jump from wall to wall.  There needs to be a manual method to move the selection tile-by-tile.  It matters where the turret's cone of fire reaches.

The AI is perhaps not superb, but so far I haven't had any serious issues with it.  At least, not yet.  Pathfinding seems okay, as long as your base isn't riddled with paths because of doors everywhere.  Picking/keeping a good crew goes along way towards avoiding frustration.  You should also invest some time in keeping them happy.  It can be difficult sometimes, but all of the information you need it given in their tabs.

Sometimes, though, the AI will do something really stupid or annoying.  Like avoiding the conveniently placed fire extinguisher in the hallway and trying to stamp out the fire.  It seems as though the extinguisher must be within the room on fire.

Of course, sometimes it helps to discover or know the AI's priorities.  With builders, for example, it's rather easy to observe their work, or lack of it, and to figure out what they prioritize.  They tend to prefer building floors before walls, and walls before any indoor work, and so on.  So, if you have a room built and while waiting for it to be filled you plan on a new hallway, the builders will drop their indoor work and go add that new section of hull first.

The game's biggest flaw, by far, then is the lack of depth.  Except for the residence and pub areas, every room has only a very small number of objects that you can place in it.  Researching does not alleviate this problem as you really just get upgraded versions of an object or an upgraded replacement model.  That's not bad, but it would be nice to have a number of topics to research (maybe based on your contact with alien visitors) that would give you new objects to use in rooms or maybe even a new room type.

This lack of depth and seeming lack of forward progression after a point seem to be the primary reasons other posters give for giving the game a thumbs down.  These really impact the length of play and replayability more than they do playability, however.

If the poor description of the game that I've given sounds like a genre that you enjoy, you'll definitely have some fun playing.  For how long I think largerly depends on how much you like exploring the mechanics of the game while you learn to play.  Experimenting with various base layouts for efficiency reasons or asthetics also adds some time and depth.

Whatever the reason for DF ceasing development, it seems pretty clear that what has been delivered is a [b]*platform*[/b] for a game.  But, of course, they were supposed to deliver a game.  Fortunately, the platform seems to be robust and moddable and even as-is provides a good amount of fun.

Judging by DF's last announcement, I doubt we'll be seeing anything more from them.  I choose to be optimistic about the game's future, though.  The quality of what they've open sourced appears good enough that I think the mod community will add a lot to the game in time.  I wish DF hadn't dropped it, but they did and there are far worse states they could have left it in.

The game does provide some long term objectives conveniently located under the "Goals" tab of the main HUD.  They are more like milestones, however, such as getting X number of crew, surviving the Mega Fleet, or killing X number of raiders.

Finally, price:  It's definitely not worth full price given the lack of depth.  I would pay anywhere between $5 and $10 for it and feel that I got my money's worth.

If you're looking for similar games, I would certainly recommend either Startopia or Evil Genius.  Startopia doesn't let you build the base, but you fill it and manage the station.  It came out some years back so it runs great on most any machine and it's a lot of fun.  Evil Genius has you building a base in your island mountain hideout.  You get to design the whole layout, rooms and hallways, similar to base building in DF-9.  Evil Genius has a lot of depth as you take on nefarious missions or as you build booby traps into your base to catch unwitting good guys.

I hope this provides a sufficiently objective view of the game.  Keep in mind that I'm still playing and making ever larger bases, so it's possible that there are some issues I've yet to encounter because my population hasn't been large enough.

This is a great concept for a game. Build and manage a space outpost with a focus on resource & personnel management and design. It has a great, fun art style, and a cheeky sense of humor. 

It's also abandoned, unfinished, and now, unloved. 

Double Fine mismanaged this project from the start, and the result is a "game" that has no goal, no progression, and few failure conditions. A "simulation" where there is little beyond the most basic needs management that can be solved in a few minutes, with no further complexity or depth to ever grow. A "product" that's buggier than The Temple of Doom. 

If you're really curious to look at what happens when a game project gets aborted but somehow thrown at the public, stillborn, then pick this game up and watch as the first few promising minutes of fun fade into unoptimized monotony. 

If not, stay away and check out either Cosmonautica for a similar "Silly Space" atmosphere, or Startopia for a better Spaceport management simulation.

This is a very simplified Dwarf Fortress style game with a sci-fi skin. The graphics are nice, and there's some humor to be found. The interface is clean, and the game is very easy to play. However, the game severely lacks content, was released as "finished" though it was no where near it, and left to the modders.

The only way I could even remotely recommend this game is if it was dirt cheap (I mean like $2 or less) AND you were interested in a colony management type game that lacked the complexity of other similar titles.

I'd recommend RimWorld (currently not on Steam), Gnomoria (I'd recommend checking out a Let's Play to learn the game), or even Prison Architect. These titles are all pretty easy to get in to, can present a good challenge that will help you learn, and actually have active developers.

In an hour and a half of play I have encountered most everything the game has to offer, as well as 3 major bugs (disappearing tiles, bugged builder AI refusing tasks, and bugged security AI which finally lost me my station). This game was promised to include many basic features of a management game that were never implemented and will never be implemented. All that is left is a very subpar blend of basic features mixed with a hint of bugs that leaves a final product that tastes poor and unfinished. 

Were it 5 dollars and still being worked on I would heartily recommend it as with bugfixing and some addition of actual content it would be a very playable game. However, at the moment there is little to be said for it. 

Additionally, and separate from the review of actual gameplay, I have to express disappointment in Double Fine for letting down their customers like this. I do not support companies that do not live up to their promises and that follow unethical practices like covering up negative reviews, and as such I would like to urge anyone else who does not wish to support these practices to avoid buying this game and to look more closely at Double Fine products in the future.

At it's current state it's not worth the $20.01 USD they are asking for it. It's unfinished and i'm sure it still has bugs. Spacebase DF-9 had to chance to be an excellent game, a fresh take on the base building genre but Double Fine dropped the ball. Now that the game has been handed over to modders 95% of people don't even know whats going on with the game. Is it being updated? Expanded? Abandoned completely? No one is sure. If you don't mind dropping $20 on an unfinished game just to play it and wonder what could have been it's a decent play for 2-3 hours. After that the game just stonewalls as you run out of new things to do. Sure you can keep playing to see how big you can get your base but it simply becomes repetitive and tedious. I suggest you do not buy this game in it's current state. Perhaps one day the community will be able to fix Double Fine's mess but until then, don't buy this game.
